title: 00:00 Cold open
text:
In September 2008, a businessman in Minnesota was talking with someone who had worked for him for fifteen years. He did not know the conversation was being recorded.

According to the Department of Justice, within the first few hours of those recordings, he was heard admitting that purchase orders were "fake". And he offered an explanation for why nobody had caught on. The only explanation, he said, was "divine intervention". It was the only way, in his words, that he and the others "could of got away with this for so long."

How long was "so long"? About fourteen years. And how much was it? By the government's count, a three point seven billion dollar Ponzi scheme. Built on paper.

title: 00:48 The central mystery
text:
This is the story of Petters Company, Incorporated, a business in the Twin Cities that told its investors it bought truckloads of consumer electronics and sold them on, at a profit, to some of the biggest retailers in America. Investors lent it money to fund those deals. They were shown the paperwork. And for years, they were paid.

But the goods in the middle of that loop were never bought. According to the evidence at trial, as the government summarized it, "no such purchases were made."

The people who lent the money were not only individuals. The government's account names an investment firm that held hundreds of millions of dollars of PCI's promissory notes. When the scheme ended, the Justice Department would call it the largest financial crime in Minnesota history.

So this film follows two questions. The first is about the money. How do you keep a lie that size afloat, through banks, investors and famous companies, for more than a decade? And where did billions of dollars actually go?

The second is about a person. Somebody inside the company had been there almost from the start, had touched the paperwork, and knew. And in September 2008, that person walked into a meeting with the authorities, with a lawyer, and offered to help bring it down.

title: 02:15 Origins
text:
The man at the center is Thomas Joseph Petters. At the time of his sentencing in 2010, the government described him as fifty-two years old and living in Wayzata, a lakeside suburb west of Minneapolis.

He was a dealmaker in consumer goods. He owned real businesses that sold real products, among them a company called Petters Warehouse Direct and another called RedTag. That matters, because it is part of why the paperwork that came later looked believable. The federal appeals court that later heard his case called him a prominent Minneapolis businessman.

In 1993, he hired an office manager. Her name was Deanna Coleman. Remember the name.

The next year, 1994, Petters formed Petters Company, Incorporated. PCI. He owned all of it. And according to the government, PCI was used for fraud from the very start.

To follow what happened next, it helps to know one ordinary business document: the purchase order. A purchase order is a buyer's written promise to buy specific goods, in a specific quantity, at a specific price. To a lender, a purchase order from a large, reliable buyer is close to a guarantee that money is coming. If a well-known chain has promised to buy a shipment, the risk in lending against that shipment looks small.

Here is the pitch, as the record describes it. PCI needed money to buy merchandise from suppliers. Once bought, that merchandise would be sold to big-box retailers, the documents named Costco and Sam's Club, at a profit. An investor who put up the money would be repaid out of that profit, with interest. To make the offer stronger, Petters often signed promissory notes and gave his personal guarantee.

It is a real kind of business. Short-term financing for goods that are already sold is ordinary, and on paper it looks safe: the buyer is a giant, the deal is short, and the goods exist. That last part is the one that wasn't true.

Investors were not paid out of profits on real sales. They were paid with money from newer investors and, the government said, "sometimes, even their own money." When a payment was due and there was nothing to pay it with, Petters stalled: promises of payment soon, excuses about retailers paying slowly, and sometimes, checks that bounced.

The government has a phrase for money paid out simply to keep investors calm: "lulling payments". They are not returns on anything. They exist to stop people asking questions, and they come out of the same pot as everyone else's money.

That's the shape of a Ponzi scheme. And a Ponzi scheme has one need that never goes away: paper. Every new dollar had to be matched by a new deal that looked real. As the money grew, so did the amount of paper someone had to make.

The government says that as the scheme went on, the office manager, Deanna Coleman, began fabricating PCI purchase orders and moving money between investors. She later admitted creating the false documents that were used to bring in investors. She received millions of dollars for it.

Over the years, she rose from office manager to an officer of the company. Keep her in mind. Of everyone in this story, she was among the closest to the paper, and to Tom Petters.

title: 05:54 Expansion
text:
By the late 1990s the paper had a weak point. A careful investor might not be satisfied with a purchase order. They might want to see the money moving, in a bank statement.

In 1999, according to the Justice Department, Petters wanted exactly that: bank statements to "verify" PCI's dealings with retailers. So he turned to a friend, Robert White, who agreed to make them. Afterwards Petters hired White and gave him the title of chief financial officer. His job, among other things, was fabricating retailer purchase orders and PCI's financial records.

Remember the name White, too. He later pleaded guilty, and when Tom Petters went on trial, Robert White testified against him.

The next weak point was money itself. If PCI said it was buying goods from suppliers, then money had to go to suppliers. And a careful investor might expect money to come back from retailers. So in 2001, Petters recruited two business associates.

The first was Larry Reynolds, who ran a company called Nationwide International Resources, NIR. He had done real deals in shoes and clothing. In 2001, Petters asked to wire money through Reynolds's bank accounts in exchange for a percentage, a "commission".

The second was Michael Catain. In early 2002, Catain created a company called Enchanted Family Buying Company and opened a business bank account. Money from Petters went in, and came back to Petters and PCI, less a commission. The government says this company did no real business. Its headquarters, according to the release, was above Catain's car wash, a few miles from Petters's own headquarters.

So now the picture an investor saw had every part. A purchase order from a famous retailer. A supplier invoice. A bank statement. Money leaving PCI for a supplier. Money coming back. On paper, the deals cleared.

Two details in the government's account show how carefully the picture was built. In some cases, investors were given false records showing that PCI had wired its own money to suppliers, so it looked as if Petters had his own money in the deals too. And investors often received PCI financial statements showing the company was owed billions of dollars by retailers. Those statements were false. The money owed by retailers did not exist, because the sales did not exist.

Here are the numbers the bank records later showed. Between January 2003 and September 2008, about twelve billion dollars flowed from the NIR account into PCI's account. Roughly the same amount again flowed in from the Enchanted Family account. Both were supposed to be suppliers, selling hundreds of millions of dollars of merchandise. The bank records showed no income for them from those sales. The money, the government said, "only flowed one way."

In April 2001, PCI had opened a new bank account that only two people were authorized to use: Tom Petters and Deanna Coleman. From 2003 to September 2008, about thirty-five billion dollars was wired into it, from investors and from the two so-called suppliers. PCI was supposedly selling merchandise to retailers. Not one of the deposits came from a retailer.

That is the heart of it. Thirty-five billion dollars in, and the customers who were supposed to be paying for the goods never paid a cent into the account, because there was nothing to pay for.

So where did it go? Some went back out to investors, to keep them content. Some went as bonuses to Petters's employees, most of whom, the government said, did not even work for PCI. Hundreds of millions funded his other companies. There was real estate for family members. Millions went to Coleman and to White. And Petters himself received tens of millions.

And then he did something that made the whole thing harder to see. He bought famous companies.

The government listed them: Fingerhut, the catalog retailer. Polaroid, the camera brand. And Sun Country Airlines. Together they became known as Petters Group Worldwide. And according to the Justice Department, they were bought with proceeds of the PCI fraud.

Think about what that did. To the public, Tom Petters was now the owner of a household name. To a lender deciding whether to put money into PCI, that was reassurance. The government put it plainly: the companies gave Petters "the appearance he needed to keep the scam going."

Those companies cost money too. Each year, the release says, PCI wrote off millions of dollars in losses from funding them. So the famous businesses that made the scheme look solid were also draining it. More investors were needed every year, to pay the old ones and to keep the empire running.

title: 11:01 Turning point
text:
By the end of 2007, the arithmetic was turning against them. The government says the conspirators were struggling to find new investors. And PCI was slow to pay hundreds of millions of dollars in promissory notes held by one of its biggest sources of money, Lancelot Investment Management, which was run by a man named Greg Bell.

Petters told Bell the delay was the retailers' fault: they were paying him late. Bell agreed to extend the payments, so the notes wouldn't go into default.

Then, in February 2008, according to the government, the two men went further. They agreed that Bell would take replacement purchase orders, from other retailers, in place of the ones Lancelot already held. And Bell suggested they also swap money back and forth, so it would look as if PCI was paying what it owed. Between late February 2008 and the day federal agents arrived, the two men made more than eighty of these "round trip" transactions. Bell later pleaded guilty for his role.

A round trip, in this sense, is money that leaves and comes back. On a bank statement, a payment from PCI to its lender looks exactly like a debt being paid. If the same money then travels back the other way, the debt hasn't really shrunk at all. Only the appearance of it has. More than eighty times in about seven months is a sign of how much appearance the scheme now needed.

In this case, the last months didn't look like a crash. They looked like a frantic effort to make it appear that nothing was wrong. And while that was happening, the one person who could see all of it made a decision.

On the eighth of September 2008, Deanna Coleman and her lawyer went to the authorities. She told them she had been helping Petters run a multi-billion-dollar Ponzi scheme for the previous ten years. She said she, Petters and Robert White had fabricated business documents to persuade investors to lend Petters money, supposedly to buy electronics for big-box retailers.

The record doesn't explain her reasons, and this film won't guess at them. The government's own description, two years later, was that she "did the right thing by bringing this fraud into the light of day."

What she offered wasn't only a confession. She agreed to work with law enforcement. And she agreed to wear a recording device, and tape her conversations with Petters and others, to back up what she was saying about White and about Petters.

Going to the authorities did not make her a bystander. By her own account she had been part of the scheme for a decade, and she would be charged for it. What she did change was who knew. From that day, the government knew what she knew, and every conversation she had with her employer could become evidence.

Think about the position that put him in. The person he had hired as an office manager in 1993, the one who had helped make the paper, who shared the bank account only the two of them could use, was now recording him.

The first few hours are already on record. "Fake." "Divine intervention." But the government says the recordings went much further than that. They "chronicled the history of the scheme." They captured the effort to keep it alive by bringing in new money and calming long-time investors. And they detailed how the conspirators planned to avoid responsibility if the fraud was ever discovered.

A plan for what to do if they were caught. And a business that was weeks, not years, from that moment. It took sixteen days.

title: 15:04 Exposure
text:
On the twenty-fourth of September 2008, agents from the FBI, the Internal Revenue Service's criminal investigators and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service executed search warrants at Petters's headquarters in Minnetonka, at his home, and at other locations. They took away a large quantity of documents and evidence.

Each of those agencies was there for a reason. The FBI investigates federal fraud. The IRS's criminal investigators follow money through bank accounts. And the Postal Inspection Service was there because, according to its own inspector in charge, the case was about "the criminal misuse of the U.S. mail". Using the mail to carry out a scheme like this is what makes it mail fraud, just as using wire transfers makes it wire fraud.

The government's later summary of the paperwork was blunt. The sales to big-box retailers that appeared in Coleman's documents were, in its words, "fictitious".

Things moved quickly after that. Within days, PCI filed for bankruptcy. And Petters, according to the government, kept reassuring investors even after the search.

Then, the government says, on the first of October he suggested to Robert White and Larry Reynolds that they flee before they could be prosecuted. Two days later, on the third of October 2008, Tom Petters was arrested and detained, after the authorities learned he had been talking about fleeing. At his sentencing in 2010, the government said he had been in custody ever since.

And the people around him began to plead guilty. Deanna Coleman was charged on the sixth of October 2008 and pleaded guilty two days later, to one count of conspiracy to commit mail fraud. By the time Petters was sentenced, Robert White, Larry Reynolds, Michael Catain and Greg Bell had also pleaded guilty for their roles in the scheme.

Petters did not. He was indicted in December 2008, and he went to trial.

The trial lasted about a month, in the fall of 2009. The government built its case on the recordings and the documents. The jury heard from people who had been inside the scheme, among them Robert White and Larry Reynolds. And it heard from Tom Petters himself, who testified in his own defense.

The judge, Richard Kyle, later gave his view of Petters's testimony in a single sentence. "It just didn't pass the smell test."

On the second of December 2009, the jury found Tom Petters guilty on all twenty counts. Ten counts of wire fraud. Three of mail fraud. One of conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud. One of conspiracy to commit money laundering. And five counts of money laundering.

In plain words: wire fraud and mail fraud are schemes to cheat people that use electronic transfers or the mail. Conspiracy means agreeing with others to commit the crime. And on money laundering, the government's account describes billions of dollars of investor money being run through business accounts like NIR's and Enchanted Family's, and back to Petters and PCI.

title: 18:19 Consequences
text:
On the eighth of April 2010, in St. Paul, Judge Kyle sentenced Tom Petters to fifty years in federal prison. The government called it the longest prison term ever ordered in a financial fraud case in Minnesota history.

Explaining the length of the term, the judge said: "I'm not satisfied that if he were released early, he wouldn't re-offend."

The U.S. Attorney for Minnesota, B. Todd Jones, spoke after the hearing. "For years," he said, "Tom Petters built his life on the shattered dreams of others." And the FBI's special agent in charge in Minneapolis said he hoped the day would mark "the start of a recovery process of sorts" for all those who had been victimized.

That September, the same judge sentenced Deanna Coleman. Her sentence was a year and a day in prison. The U.S. Attorney said her help had been "extremely valuable", but that she "still had to pay a price for her own wrongdoing."

He went on to say that the sentence reflected her choice, in the release's words, of "conscious over loyalty and greed": her choice to come forward rather than stay silent.

Fifty years for the man who ran it. A year and a day for the woman who helped him run it, and then helped end it. That gap shows how much a cooperating witness can matter to a prosecution.

Petters appealed, challenging his conviction and his sentence. On the ninth of December 2011, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld both.

In September 2010, the government said he was being held at the federal penitentiary in Leavenworth, Kansas.

And the money? PCI's bankruptcy case, in the federal bankruptcy court in Minnesota, ran on for years after the conviction. As late as 2019 and 2020, the trustee for PCI was still in court, suing to recover money that had been paid out before the collapse.

The famous companies were caught up in the collapse too. Polaroid, one of the household names that had made the scheme look solid, filed for bankruptcy in December 2008, in the same Minnesota court.

It is worth going back to the government's own summary of the scheme. Investors were shown purchase orders, invoices, bank records and financial statements. Each one was a document someone had made. For about fourteen years, the paperwork was the product.

That leaves a question the people who lost money have every reason to ask: how did it last so long? The records this film relies on describe what was done to deceive investors, and they treat the lenders as the people deceived. They don't name anyone outside the scheme who knew, and this film doesn't suggest that any lender, auditor or retailer did. What they do show is how much effort went into making every document match every other one.

And it didn't end with an audit, or a whistle from outside. It ended with someone on the inside, who had made the paper herself, deciding to walk into a room and tell the authorities, and then letting a recorder run.

She was not the first. In March 1973, in a very different company, a former officer took a secret of his own to an investment analyst. What he said sounded impossible: that the assets of a big life insurance and mutual fund company were vastly overstated, the result of fraud. The analyst set out to find out if it was true. And the person who ended up in trouble with the regulators was not the one who had run the fraud. That's the next film.
